doc.title: Dave Frishberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001

title: Repertoire and the union hall
summary: Repertoire was his arsenal; at the union hall on Wednesdays you had to say you knew all the tunes, and at sessions you blew hard in private.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Well I guess I shouldn’t say especially to a piano player. For everyone. Because we were all, you know it was the days when you said yes to everything. And there was no gig too meager or demeaning to say no to. You know? You said yes. And therefore you had a lot of adventures and also learned a lot of stuff. But you needed to be prepared. And repertoire was your arsenal of things that you brought to the table. So when you’re looking at the union, you’d be down at the union hall on Wednesday afternoons, you know about the union hall?
Yeah, but I want to hear how this worked.

And then you’d be hanging out there just so you’d get your face known you know. And the musicians would take you by the hand and they’d lead you around and this is Irving Bower or whatever his name is you know, and he’s got a board and he’s writing down things and he says, “You know all the tunes?” And then you’re supposed to say yes, you know. Some people would say no. Some people would say all but one.
Hope they don’t call that one.

Yeah. So you had to know songs. And then of course at the sessions you learned repertoire, jazz repertoire. But the idea at the jam sessions was to just blow your brains out. You were there to blow choruses and just play hard, as hard as you could as a jazz player you know. And it was all in private. It was all for the visceral pleasure of the
whole thing. Also it was socially interesting. I met a lot of people there for the first time in lofts.
